title-group.article-title: Can Hypernasality be Reliably Rated Using the American English Phrase Sample as a Part of the Cleft Audit Protocol for Speech-Augmented-Americleft Modification (CAPS-A-AM) Protocol?

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: The American English Phrase Sample is an alternative repetition stimulus that can be used as a part of the Cleft Audit Protocol for Speech-Augmented-Americleft Modification.

sec.title: Problem:
sec.p: Reliability for rating hypernasality is unknown when the phrase sample is used.

sec.title: Solution:
sec.p: Assessed intra- and interrater reliability for rating hypernasality.

sec.title: What we did:
sec.p: Intrarater reliability was k = 0.76–0.91 and interrater reliability was k = 0.63–0.77. The phrase sample had the same reliability for rating hypernasality as the sentence sample.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hypernasality severity rating is the primary perceptual outcome used in many studies assessing resonance following primary palate repair1 and secondary surgery to treat velopharyngeal insufficiency.2 The Cleft Audit Protocol for Speech-Augmented-Americleft Modification (CAPS-A-AM) is a commonly used perceptual evaluation protocol in the United States to rate hypernasality.3 Protocols for assessing perceptual speech characteristics must have high inter- and intrarater reliability to ensure postoperative outcome measurements and clinical diagnoses are accurate and consistent, no matter which speech-language pathologist conducts the evaluation. Reliability for rating hypernasality using the CAPS-A-AM protocol was established with 5- to 7-year-old children repeating sentences as the repetition task. Intrarater reliability for rating hypernasality was very good (k = 0.84–0.85) and interrater reliability was good (k = 0.70–0.71).3

An alternative controlled sample was developed at the phrase level by SLPs involved in the Americleft Speech Project3 to use with younger children or children with developmental delays who cannot imitate the longer sentences, as shown in Table 1. The American English Phrase Sample (AEPS) consists of 24 2-to-3-word phrases. The phrases were designed according to Henningsson et al.4 universal parameters for assessing cleft palate speech by (1) sampling all oral pressure consonants, (2) limiting each utterance to 1 target consonant, and (3) controlling for high and low vowels. Nasal phonemes are assessed separately from the oral pressure phonemes. Each phrase is loaded with a specific target sound in the initial and final position of a word embedded within a phrase.

Our cleft team (JCW and KNC) adopted the phrase sample into clinical practice more than five years ago as an alternative repetition task as a part of the CAPS-A-AM protocol; however, the reliability for rating hypernasality when the phrase sample is used with young children is currently unknown. The purpose of the present study was to assess intra- and interrater reliability for rating hypernasality when the phrase sample was used as the repetition task as a part of the CAPS-A-AM protocol. The null hypothesis was there was no difference in reliability for rating hypernasality between the sentence and phrase samples.

sec.title: Method
sec.p: This cross-sectional study received institutional review board (IRB) approval from Arizona State University IRB No. STUDY00016321. Informed consent procedures were conducted with legal guardians as a part of a larger study prior to collecting the speech samples. The consent included analysis of speech data, specifically perceptual ratings, consonant inventory, syllable structure, error analysis, and percent consonants correct. The perceptual ratings of hypernasality from the larger study were used for the present study.

Participants were recruited as part of a larger prospective study of children with and without cleft palate between the ages of 3;0 and 4;11 (years; months). The children were recruited through local daycare centers, local preschool centers, flyer distribution throughout the university campus, word-of-mouth, and a metropolitan cleft and craniofacial center. Sixty-seven children were enrolled in the larger study at the time of this analysis and were included in the present study—37 children without cleft palate and 30 children with a history of a cleft palate repaired in infancy.

Each child completed a recorded speech sample that included 2–3 min of conversation, counting 1–10 or 1–20, and phrase repetition. Children were prompted to imitate the numbers if they were unable to complete the counting task. The speech samples were video recorded using a Zoom Q8 handy Video Recorder and an Audio-Technica Short-Shotgun Microphone on a boom stand within 6 inches of the child’s mouth.5 The recordings were deidentified, assigned a participant ID, and subsequently uploaded to Dropbox for rating. All participants completed the assessment protocol in English. The components of the elicited speech sample using the sentence-level stimuli compared to the phrase-level stimuli are shown in Table 2.

Three SLPs (KML, CLS, and NRW) from 3 different institutions rated hypernasality after listening (audio-only) to the phrase repetition task for all 67 speech samples as part of the methodology for a larger study. All 3 SLPs had ≥7 years of experience rating hypernasality. The SLPs rerated a subset of samples (n = 7; 10%) to calculate intrarater reliability. None of the SLPs were involved in the clinical care of any of the participants. Hypernasality was rated on the 5-point ordinal scale used in the CAPS-A-AM protocol as follows: 0 = none; 1 = minimal (slight increase in nasal resonance); 2 = mild (evident on high vowels); 3 = moderate (evident on all vowels); 4 = severe (evident on vowels and voiced consonants). The SLPs could listen to the speech sample as many times as needed to rate hypernasality.

sec.title: Statistical Methods
sec.p: The original CAPS-A-AM reliability study computed intra- and interrater reliability using a weighted kappa statistic.3 For equal comparison, inter- and intrarater reliability was calculated in the present study using the same weighted kappa statistic and weighting assignments.3 Statistical analyses were performed using the statistical software package Python 3.8 scikit-learn library that allows for quadratic weighting.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Intrarater reliability across the 3 raters was k = 0.91, 0.95, and 0.76, indicating good to very good reliability. Interrater reliability was k = 0.77 for raters 1 and 2, k = 0.77 for raters 1 and 3, and k = 0.63 for raters 2 and 3, indicating good reliability. Table 3 shows the intra- and interrater reliability ratings using the sentence sample from the original CAPS-A-AM reliability study with 5- to 7-year-olds compared to intra- and interrater reliability ratings using the phrase sample with 3- to 4-year-olds from this study.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In the present study, intrarater reliability for rating hypernasality using the phrase sample was good to very good. Intrarater reliability in the present study was consistent with the reliability reported in the original CAPS-A-AM study (k = 0.76–0.95 vs k = 0.84–0.85). Similarly, interrater reliability was consistent between studies (k = 0.63–0.77 vs k = 0.70–0.71). These findings suggest that clinicians and researchers who use hypernasality as their primary outcome measure can use the phrase sample with the same level of reliability to rate hypernasality as the sentence sample.

The consistent reliability found in this study between the phrase and sentence samples is likely due to the speech samples being rated on the same ordinal scale and the samples being developed based on the same parameters. Clinicians should ensure that when using the phrases clinically and in research, they also elicit all components of the perceptual speech sample including conversation, counting, and the repetition task. This allows for a full sampling of consonants and vowels across three different speaking contexts for hypernasality to be reliably rated.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: The present study only assessed reliability for rating hypernasality, as this is the primary outcome used by many research studies.1,2 Further research is needed to assess reliability for rating other perceptual parameters between the sentence and phrases such as audible nasal emission, hyponasality, and cleft speech characteristics.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Hypernasality reliability can be rated using the AEPS as a part of the CAPS-A-AM protocol.
